# Olive Oil and Stroke Risk: Evidence Review

**Conclusion: The evidence supports this claim, particularly for higher-quality studies.** Multiple lines of research — cohort studies, a meta-analysis, and a randomized controlled trial — consistently link higher olive oil consumption to reduced stroke risk, though the strength of causal certainty varies by study design.

**Observational evidence:** A French cohort study of over 7,000 people aged 65+ (Bordeaux/INSERM researchers) found that regular olive oil consumers had lower stroke risk than non-consumers; a secondary analysis using plasma oleic acid (a marker of olive oil intake) found those with the highest levels had a 73% lower stroke risk ([Biospace](https://www.biospace.com/olive-oil-linked-to-lower-stroke-risk-university-of-bordeaux-study); [Times of Malta](https://timesofmalta.com/article/Olive-oil-could-lower-stroke-risk-study-finds.371508)). However, this is observational data, meaning healthier lifestyle habits among olive-oil consumers could partly explain the association.

**Meta-analysis evidence:** A rigorous meta-analysis combining case-control, cohort, and intervention studies (Martínez-González et al., *British Journal of Nutrition*) examined olive oil's relationship to CHD and stroke across nearly 39,000 stroke-related participants, finding an inverse association between olive oil intake and stroke risk ([Cambridge/BJN](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/olive-oil-consumption-and-risk-of-chd-andor-stroke-a-metaanalysis-of-casecontrol-cohort-and-intervention-studies/79A90337470271D8A8CE2FDC77BD869E)).

**Strongest evidence — randomized trial:** The PREDIMED trial, a large randomized controlled trial, is the most methodologically robust source here. It found that a Mediterranean diet enriched with extra-virgin olive oil (compared to a control diet) significantly reduced incidence of stroke, myocardial infarction, and cardiovascular mortality ([ULPGC/PREDIMED PDF](https://accedacris.ulpgc.es/bitstream/10553/44645/1/extravirgin_olive_oil.pdf)).

**Caveat:** Some sources note that in populations where olive oil intake was historically low, other Mediterranean diet components (vegetables, whole grains) may share credit for protective effects, making it hard to isolate olive oil's independent contribution in purely observational settings.

**Bottom line:** The claim is well-supported, especially by RCT evidence (PREDIMED), making it one of the stronger diet-disease associations in nutrition science.
